Winters were often severe and snow-banks sometimes mounted as high as the top of the gabel roof: but poor, dear Father took care be- fore the cold weather set in, to bank well wherever he might, so that we were fairly comortable no matter how the wind howled or the mercury sank. You'll be wondering soon, more than before if I keep on in this strain, how it might be called a mansion. Well, every decent mansion has a chapel of some demensions .... Ours was at times all chapel, and at times something of a church. As long as we lived in that little abode - a "hovel" possibly outside but clean and neat as a palice within - we were wont to say our morning and night prayers to- gether; and on Sundays at 10 a.m., Father woud read Mass Prayers. Of course when the weather permitted and the roads were anyway decent he would trudge away to church about six miles taking short cuts dis- tant. Then Ellie or James or one of the others would lead the prayers. Sometimes they seemed pretty long. It was on such a Sunday that Papa and Jime had gone to church when we saw the black clous of smoke ris- ing from the far side of some of the hills off to the South. The wind was pretty strong too and poor dear Mother seemed quite anxious - giv- ing instructions what to do and getting ready for what must have look- ed probable, a burn out. Ellie scratched a little "hoe-mark" out in front of the house and sprinkled holy water in it about half way down to the barn. By this time the fire was crackling through the grass and brush this side of Lam's Road and the smoke rolled over our heads in thick, dark clouds. Then the barn took fire, some ten rods east of the house, and we all went down, carying some bed-clothes, to the lone tree that for a long time stood in the middle of the original four-acre field. This, I think, must have been about the second summer we lived in Trimbelle. Because we had a new field, if I remember right, of about six acres and the great oaks over to the N. East, among which the prairie chickens at first played and danced were gone; And as we were huddled together under said lone tree (my own little face hidden in Mother's dress from the smoke) I heard Mother saying in ac- cents of relief: "Thanks be to God! some of the neighbors have come and let the pig out". It was a big white one and had broken out of the pen itself where it had been a contented prisoner right near the barn. We saw it running for safety. Papa and James got home shortly after Noon and some of the neighbors came to sympathise with us. It seemed a fresh clear day but our barn was in ruins and the hills were black in every direction, except our fields and up to the N.T. where the fire did not cross the highway. In fact, I do not think it crossed said highway except to burn our barn. Two slight vallies joined at the foot of theN.E. corner of the garden and formed quite a ravine running nothword between the old and the new fields. This was joined by one or two others from the side in its course down to the "Big Ravine", a beautiful valley, that curved northword and then eastword among some of the most picturisque hills that I have ever seen -- off to loose itself in the bottoms of the Trimbelle. These hills and low- lands formed a great part of our pasture-lands where we boys, especial- ly Maurice and I till he leaft for Stillwater to study, used to watch the cattle and study our catechism. Sometimes we'd roll rocks down the hill-sids - great amusement for boys! - or pick perries or fish and swim till the cattle would stray away and get into mischief and then we would have our own anxieties finding them. Sometimes we got our medicine for carelessness; more frequently, perhaps, we es

Just a line while I have time to gratulate you and wish you every blessing. Mary Casey just phoned - is coming out this p.m. to have a little visit, before going back to-night to camp. .. Her mother Emma scalded herself recently rather badly and James Jr. had an operation oo his les. ... . otherwise things seem about as usual on the Coast. I wrote Fr. Edward a few days ago - have not bad word from him in a long time. I know he has very little time for himself - what quite pleases him, I think. God bless you now and all my old friends in "City of fine Schools, Villas & Terraces"

God bless you and I hope you are well -- trying at least to be contented. I started to write you on the beautiful Feast of our Blessed Mother, the Immaculate Conception; being as it was the 42nd anniversary of the happy day of my vocation to St. Bonaventure's. Thanks be to God and the same His Blessed Immaculate Mother. As often happens, however, I did not get far with my letter that day; so now, before the octave passes, I'll try once more. This I've wanted to do out of gratitude for such a vocation to such an order and, I might say, especially for the grace of learning so quickly to love the Order -- notwithstanding my prejudice on coming hither as I did, half against my will. I offered my rosary this morning out in the crisp, moon-light air for your intentions and your guidance. I am confident that though, like the rest of us -- poor children of Eve -- you have your difficulties, your temptations, your falls even, and your occasional little triumphs, our dear Lord will keep you from serious blunderings. In fact, not only this, but notwithstanding your very sad blunderings in the past -- possibly worse than my own, possibly not so bad -- I still hope and pray that in the few years left us, you may do something to make up for lost time; something to save your soul and gain the one vic- tory, the one crown, the only triumph really worthy a rational creature's every effort. The "few years" did I say ??? Who can tell? We hope so, of course, if it be God's holy will; but O! How uncertain! . . it may be tomorrow they'll say of you or of me or of each of us: "He is gone." If either of us live ten years longer it will be passing the old-age mark for our clan. And after all, what's the difference if we only be ready? Nay, if it be tomorrow or fifty years hence, if we only save our immortal souls? What's the difference? But dear Father Maurice Joachim: I hardly know what to say or to think of your proposition to write back to your old diocese, to a prelate you've possibly never met and who has possibly never heard of Father Joachim. Naturally you would hope to be received with open arms, -- dreaming as you probably do, of some cozy little place just smiling across the Wisconsin hills at you. Ah dear Fr. Maurice Joachim! You may be sure, such would be only dreaming. Your age and your experience shoul rather exclude such dreams as belonging to the long ago. This we might think especially, considering your years of dreaming when and how you might get away from the world to a monastery. Think of it, dear Father Joachim Nearly five and thirty years back, while still in the mail service, you wrote on the feast that since has become your own name-day: 11 .. . This is my plan' and I want you to let me know what you think of it. 11 . . . .I'll try it out for a year or so and if it goes then I'll join yours or some other holy order. If it don't go, I'll be a lay-brother. And if that fails, then by George I'll get married and go out West and be as useful to God and man as I can, a secular I'll never be." You wrote that from Prairie Avenue, Chicago. I showed your letter to dear, old Father Bonaventure, ex-Provincial at the time, and Fr. Superior in Yonkers, where I was stationed (for 14 years following). May his dear soul rest in peace. He was pleased with your letter and said: " ... He has good intentions. Tell him to go ahead .. " The next letter I received from you, you were back in college after twenty years vacation. This time in Berlin -- now Kitchener -- Ontario. Your handwriting on the envelope presaged your sentiments within: " ... I have found the peace again I looked for so long, and in this I feel amply re- paid for the sacrifice it took to give up everything." What a practical experience, -- a grace to convince you that sacrifice willingly made for God's sake is always a small sacrifice for results sure to follow. Deo Gratias! Dear Brother -- Dear Father M. J. : You've long since wanted to be a real missionary. So has your brother whom you have led (according to age, three years in advance) wished to be indeed a missionary ... When are we to start? Whither shall we turn to find a field wherein our zeal will be profitable to souls and appreciated? Shall we go to the ends of the earth, or shall we, convinced that Charity, rightly ordered, begins at home? Shall we begin right in our own hearts? As, dear Maurice; if, "what we do for our own souls is 100% for the glory of God, then surely we don't need to go far for mission work. After all, we have just one soul -- and only -- that we must save. Should we in the end save everyone else in the whole world and not save our own soul, what would it profit us? . (What wretchedly poor work! Interrupted again and again: I'd do it all over had I another day. Deo Gratias! O Brother Dear! Why are we all so stupid? We are all alike in a way. We worry our heads and our hearts about many things like Martha and almost totally undervalue the in- vitation -- most beautiful of all -- "learn of me because I am meek and humble of heart." Mary the Penitent understood it and Jesus praised her for her appreciation. . It seems to me that, were we only to correspond to God's graces, continually being showered down on everyone of us, we would be able to pass from being great sinners one day to be great saints the next. The following are a few lines from a letter received a day or two back. It is from a one-time leading religious and writer, who seemingly is having a purgatory of things these past few years. " ... to the good God who must sorrow even more than I do over this situation, "I have indeed come to know that I am nothing, I have nothing and can do nothing, and all that re- mains is a tiny flicker of a weak will 'to want' to remain faith- ful and persevere, no matter what the cost." I am enclosing a copy of the rhyme-letter you gave to Fr. ex-Provincial two years ago. It will do you good to read it over whenever you be inclined to play with "the blues." Friends of ours here offered to make a number of copies to send to any- one I might wish. Besides this, I cam across a description of dear, old Father's death, written shortly after he died. Wishing to get a copy of it before I'd send the original to the oldest of the Family, these friends made copies of it too, one of which I am herewith enclosing. Incidentally, Christmas Eve will be the tenth anniversary of the writer's funeral. R.I.P. I believe you had the Mass, with six of her brothers pall-bearers -- two of whom you had the privilege, sad as it must have been, of laying to rest just a month later. R.I.P.

The following letter from my eldest sister, Mrs. Ella (Casey) Traynor, who taught me my ABCs and next to dear Mother my prayers, describes dear Father's last struggles and beautiful death. The writer herself has since passed away, having been burried Christmas Eve 1928. May their dear souls rest in the peace of the saints!

God bless you and yours. I've been trying to get in touch you for weeks. Am sending you herewith Jim's letter received last Monday. There is since I started this card just a dozen people came in waiting. I wanted to tell you about the jubilee we had out in Royal Oak. There was surely a grand crowd . . about fifty priests -- bishops and sisters. (3 Capuchins)

God bless you and yours -- including my poor self I hope. I received your welcome letter yesterday and, while there is a silent note therein of dis- satisfaction, that I can hardly be surprized at or blame you for, yet I am more than pleased and I thank God for what, in my opinion, must please Heaven better than any success you ever had -- or could have without it -- on missions, parishes or catechism teachings. Thank God for your tone of patient resignation, at once a great promoter and a fruit of Christian humility. God himself has provide in your present trying circumstances, a mill in His wisdom and in His mercy for your refinement in these virtues that pleas Him most. It seems to me a most hopeful indication if, notwithstanding your blunders as well as your successes for three and thirty years in the holy Priesthood -- in the brunt of the warfare, therefore -- and especially under your present trying circumstances, you can still sigh: "Non nobis Domine! non nobis ... ". Its God and His holy grace more than anything else that we ought thak. Blessed be His Holy Name! About a year ago, on occasion of his 60th anniversary as a priest the renowned Pastor of Ironton, Ohio-outstanding lecturer and writer -- Father Cotter, told of his saintly and venerated sister then recently deceased, that when he had come into her presence after just hearing all kinds of laudations on occasion of his jubilee ten years before, she earnestly and honestly exclaimed: "O James! How we ought to thank God that for these fifty years He has never per- mitted you to/any real scandal." So dear Brother, Fr. Joachim: let us be grateful to God for everything -- the knocks we get as well as the consolations. ... and do not blame the Father Chaplain too severely if he seem unduly exacting, etc. Of all positions he has one that in my opinion must at times be on his nerves. Who can doubt that at times, now and then at least, he must be up against delicat cases? Rather continue to pray for him and for all connected with the institution. They all have their difficulties and there is none without their defects. Who is to blame? .... God could have founded His Church and left/under the supervision of angels, that have no human faults and weaknesses. But who can doubt that as it stands today, consisting of and under the supervision of poor sinners -- successors to ignorant fishermen -- that it is more of a "standing miracle" than in any other way think- able? Could not the same thing be said of practically every charitable institution? It seems to me that our task-our privilege -- ought to be just to help along in some trifling way. In a way, the big things are really not so important. There is always some one ready to take care of such -- even if, like Judas, they make a botch of it. But what a privilege to take care of trifles that only our guardian-angels enjoy and God himself can divinely appreciate! -- sweeping, pulling weeds, picking potato-bugs, etc. etc. How trifling! or suffering little mortifications, offering little ejaculatory prayers, dropping a word of sympathy, etc. all trifles. But "trifles make perfection and perfection is never a trifle. Perfection is divine. In God's sight -- who can doubt-the world itself is made up of trifles . If we were but a tenth as appreciative as we ought to be, how happy we would be simply in our creation and the faculties we're endowed with and the divine promises etemal reward!

God bless you and yours -- my poor self I hope included. I received your letter yesterday and, while there is a silent note therein of dissatisfaction that I can hardly be surprized at or blame you for, yet I am more than pleased and I thank God for the wonderful progress you've made in what must, in my opinion, please Heaven better than all your success on the Rockey-Mountain Missions or at catechism in parishes or hospitals, etc. In other words, your profiting by the outstanding opportunity God himself, in His wisdom and mercy has been providing for you in the mill of humiliation. -- "No humiliation, no humility; no humility, no real virtue." (S. Ber - nard) . It's God and His holy grace more than anything else we ought thank that you, after three and thirty years in the Holy Priesthood, in the brunt of the "warfare, therefore, you can still cling to your motto: "NON NOBIS DOMINE NON NOBIS !" This we may say especially under your present circumstances to say -- and to act what we proclaim to God: "Not to us O Lord! not to us, but to Thy Name be the glory given !" About a year ago, on occasion of his 60th anniversary to the Priesthood, the re- nowned Pastor of Ironton, Ohio -- outstanding writer and lecturer -- Father Cotter, told of his saintly and venerated sister, then recently deceased, that when he had come into her presence after just hearing all kinds of laudations on occasion of his Jubilee ten years before, she exclaimed earnestly and honestly: "O James ! How we ought thank God that for these fifty years He has never permitted you to give any real scandal !" So, dear Brother Maurice, Fr. Joachim: do not blame poor Father Chaplain if he seems unduly exacting, etc. If he were not a conscientious priest he would hardly be in such an ex- tremely trying position. For who can doubt that at least now and then, he has delicate cases, etc? Rather continue to pray for him -- and for all concerned with the institution. They all have their difficulties and there is none of them without defects. Who is to blame? God could have established His Church under supervision of angels that have no faults or weaknesses. But who can doubt that as it standsToday, consisting of and under the supervision of poor sinners -- successors to the "poor Fisher-men of Galilee", the Church is a more outstanding miracle than any other way? Quite the same might be said of any charitable institution. So keep up your prayers and patience and resignation for God's blessed sake; and be sure He is watching all and will never be outdone in generosity. Nor will He ever fail in what He assures : "He that humbleth himself shall be exalted." Who has not sadly experienced the opposite: "He that exalteth himself shall be humbled"? How can we ever thank the merciful God that we still have a chance to humble ourselves and to merit!

God bless you and yours. I meant to write you a letter to-day a number of times and now its 11 P.M. Well, how can we thank the Good God for all His patience with us and all the graces lavished upon each? ! Thirty-two yrs back Oct. 2 -- we Fr. E'd, Jim (R. I. P.) and I awoke in the "Bad-Lands of N. D." Jim's keen eye espied a kyote scrambling up one of the peculiar formations to which he called our attention . - How short it now seems! What changes since! But looking forward, what changes are ahead in half 32 years! ? Let us bless and adore the Providence that has kept us and have all in His hands who keep tally on the hairs of our heads. . . and the sighes and the breaths we take -- and notwithstanding our blunders and stupid- ity still plans on for our best. Only this P. M. I received, Via Detroit, Mich, my own letter to Fr. E'd, back from the Phil- ippines. He ought to know what's in it by tomorrow. I forget. Mail-marked five months tomorrow. I just reddressed it and added a 3rd Air Stamp. I am praying the dear, Good God to guide you whither you'll find it more congenial than you resigned yourself to the past few years. Nevertheless dear Fr. M. Joachim, its good for us. I just found this as I left it several days ago. to reach you by this Sunday and here it is 9:30 P. M. got back half an hour back from old people's Home in Staten Island . . God's blessing to yourself and Fr. Edw'd -- Rt. to all I meant - just Rev.

God bless you and yours. Have just written Fr. J. O'Donnell -- also answered cur poor sister-in-law. Thank God she and Florence too seem to be trying bravely to keep up -- following close (at least) to the straight narrow path -- the chalk-line to happiness. Try and drop a card to poor Fr. O'Donnell. In his case, as I just wrote him, like everybody else's, it is the enemy of our souls that is always trying to minimize and to hide the surpassing advantages by which everyone of us are surrounded. God help us!

Brother, is the announcement of the same happy event to near relatives and friends who would be naturally more or less acquainted with the ups and downs that poor dear Father Maurice was known to have gone through, and the more than ordinary disappointments, humiliations, ambitions and sometimes triumphs of his over 81 years. Even among such near and dear ones, however, -- though the ideal seems to be common in the "Island of Saints" -- comparatively few ever knew of the fact that our dear Parents had mutually dreamed of the privilege of being parent to a Priest in their family, which ideal would seem to have buoyed their hopes from the earliest years wherein they recognized holy matrimony as a state of life in which to serve God and help Him to save souls. Furthermore; when the writer was in his seventh year and there were three brothers among the five dear-ones ahead of him, it just seemed self - understood as though planned before his birth that Maurice was to be the Priest. Not only was this the case in our immediate family and relatives, but our neighboring children often spoke of it and seemed to revere him as so fortunately destined and chosen. So much was this true that some one even at that time and perhaps earlier, began to wonder if possibly there couldn't be two priests in a family -- hardly hesitating that he would be the other himself. 3ORI NOV. 10, 1867; ORDAINED JUNE 9TH 1911; DIED JAN. 12TH 1949. God bless you . I hope you are well - you and yours. Though it is just striking 11 p.m. I want to at least start you a few words before re- tiring after this busy day, and in a way even for me eventful day. For yourself of course, and for every one whose privilege it has been to be in immediate touch with the Eucharistic Congress out there in the Philippines it has been no doubt more than eventful. However, we here get the announce- ments over the radeo about 8 a.m. in Detroit and heard the Holy Father's own voice and benediction. His conclusion with benediction seemed to be really: ". in Nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti". I hope you may send us details worth while. The press here - even the Catholic part of it has been very tame so far about this great event. I hope to learn that it surpassed in solemnity and impressiveness even the grandeur, etc, of the Congress in Ireland, of which Cardinal Hayes is said to have remarked: "It surpassed the insurpassible". Having barely missed going to that great event I almost dreamed of my going this one in '37. Had it been closer to the time of your jubilee I would possibly have been sent. I have not been anxious, however, to under- take such an expensive and extraordinary trip, - unless of course some ad- ditional duty should waft me thither. That I was sent to help Father Mau- rice to celebrate, seemed quite appropriate at the time. Now it seems to have been fortunate. In fact I believe quite a few blessings came as a con- sequence to myself & more. I have a letter from a certain ascetic invalid, Mary Kerrman of St. Elizabeth Hospital, Elizabeth New Jersey, I want to in- close ... well, just as a sample. Asking for details about the great Congress, I hope you may not think of taking as a criterion the example of the present writer. I am sure you expected some report about our visit in New York last June. As a matter of fact I started more than once to give you a short summary of my ten-day di- version, on that occasion. Hoping that it may not be without interest, I'll try just briefly to give you an idea about the whole affair even though be- lated. Father M. Joachim seems to have spoken to Rev. Father Provincial about it some months before, and the latter told me it would be alright. I started off Wednesday evening June 3rd. The evening and night were ideal in sun-set and moon-light, we crossed the Niagara about 13 miles above the Falls but even at that the waters seemed to be swirling on to as if rushing to a tragedy. Though I slept very little I was not tired when the dawn re- vealed we were descending the Mchawk Valley stopping only once or twice before reaching Albany. Then down the Hudson to Garrison just across from Westpoint Military Academy. Walking to the Monastery about a mile below, I said holy Mass close to 9 a.m. Deo Gratias! I found things so inviting afterwords that I decided to rest there a day. The grounds are spacious to say the least and I might say almost dangerously grand. Originally there were, I believe over 400 acres. They soled quit a piece of it includ- ing the Sugar-loaf Mountain - one of the most beautiful along the Hudson, to help defray building of the new Monastery. After vespers I went for a hyke. Only half determined to climb the Mt., and feeling more like myself in the holy habit I just went as I was. How- ever, the air was so salubrious as I ascended and the breezes and shade so inviting that I pushed on and up through under brush and across paths and roads till I found none of these any more. Finally, after quite a climb through almost trackless brush, mostly not dense, I reached the rather unin- viting top and climbed a gentle evergreen to look out over the canoy (canopy) of sumit foliage. The scenry was grand, as far as it went, but in remembrance of the beautiful views, decade age so familiar to us, from Mt. Saint Helen and before that from the gentler hills of old Trimbelle, I soon found it monotnous and disapointing in hoped-for views. So I climed down after a little and started down the face of old Sugar-loaf. I think it was a totally unexplored route; but aided by a strong emergency staff, and dreamings of similar climb- ings - though on smaller scales - 60 or more years ago, I made the descent with some narow escapes and a few harmless bumps on rear fenders. Deo Gratias. It was close to supper-time when I got back to the monastery, and I need not tell you I had an appetite. We had recreation that evening which ... very happy and its a long time since I slept sounder than that night. Next day, finding he had some extra business in New York, Fr. Guardian brought me down by auto. We crossed over between Sugar-loaf and the now famous Mt. of Atonement and went down over the High-lands. It was quite a descent indeed. After we had gone down so many hills that I was beginning to think we were coming close to normally level ground we suddenly curved past a sign: "Hill". I had to smile as we dashed past it and over the top, the dri- ver seemingly knowing every inch and bump ahead till again and again we con- tinued to make inclines. At about 11 a.m. we passed through picturesque old Yonkers and still down with, few little ups. Via the Western Driveway past the Washington Bridge (over the Hudson), and over Canal Street past "Office of the Irish World" we reached Our Lady of Sorrows Monastery just before the noon Angelus and dinner greeting. Only after dinner that day was I informed that Fr. Sol. was supposed to give the sermon of the jubilee solemnity. Luckily my next neighbor at table had asked me a week or so before: "Did you get an invitation to preach the jubilee sermon?", and remembering my surprise the morning before the Golden Jubilee in Seatle, by the announcement in church that "Father Bernard will give the sermon", I did not mind the task, having thought things over what to say. In fact I felt it quit a privilege even to get back again into the old pulpit that I had not seen for near fifteen years, and to address old friends & new. Well the jubilee passed, as do all things temporal, and seemingly everyone was satisfied as to its impressiveness, etc. Just one in all con- cerned was not exactly satisfied that I knew, but neither did he complain. Rather he thanked God that it went as well as it did and hoped he might do better another time. Besides friends from Yonkers and Harlem and Brooklyn, etc, two of our cousins - nuns from Waltham, Mass., were at the Solemn Mass that day. The following days the Rev. brothers visited the brethren and friends together in East New York, Harlem, Yonkers, Hoboken, N.J., etc. We went also to see Thomas Ford of the Irish World. He is the only survivor of the sons of the great founder that old beacon-light of culture - of pa- triotism at once and of religion. I knew them all in former years together with their still surviving sister. He seemed pleased at our call. Friday noon I went to Albany and thence by bus to some friends in Watervleit just across from Troy. They took me back to Albany for the night "Wolverine" and that reached Detroit about 7 a.m. Saturday, Deo Grat! Of course I need not inform you of the Provincial Chapter and the many changes that followed. One of these was that Fr. M. E.J. was transferred to Marathon, Wis. After stoping here a few days on the way thither, and a few weeks in the new - St. Anthony Monastery - he seems to have quite enjoyed a week or so vacation. This he spent mostly visiting old friends, and scenes of long ago -- in the majority of cases of course, not the same as painted on memory's canvas. Well, if they only reminded him of ups and downs of our in- nocent days, congratulations. In a way I think I would like to have been with him; Though as a rule it suffices me to think back and consider the lonesome changes that were taking place in old Trimbelle even before we left, and that I know to have taken place since, both there and about the Mt. St. Helen Home - the little green garden of the Saint Croix Valley. It suffices me, I wanted to say, to think of these changes by the hand of time. and after the dear Angel of death, to lift my longings of heart and soul from such days "and dreamings never more to be", and to focus them again and again on ideals that are not" .. wrecked on the shores of the real", and neither, sleep like a dream in a grave". Well Dear Edward; you are no doubt surprized at the length of this letter. I hope it is grave enough not to scandalize. I hardly need say I finished it Sunday night after starting as the clock struck 11. I pro- bably had not finished and it would have gone as so many others, and I behaved myself a little better, physically, and not been sent ... a cell recuperating. Just a little cold Thank God. I'm posted for the 5 o'clock Mass tomorrow ( 1st Sunday of Lent) So I'll just say

God bless you and yours. But I learn from a clipping that Mrs. Doonan sent me recently that I may address you hereafter as Rt. Rev. Msgr. In that case and since I've been informed of the dignity otherwise I want to say God bless you again; and in as much as it probably is for the glory of His holy Name and that of our Blessed Mother Mary, Let me say also, Congratulations! About this, however, more another time. Well a few days later a telegram from the Monastery on West 31st St. N. Y. City to the efect that Fr. wanted to get into St. Elizabeth Hospital ... what to do, so far he had failed .... Father Provincial had gone to Calvary Wis., in the mean time and on reception of the telegram by special delivery, wired the Fr. Guard- ian in 31st St. to do all in his power to help Father to get into St. Elizabeth's or some other like it. Poor Fr. M.J., however, could not be located. ... Heart-sick, as I imagine he must have been, at disa- pointment after disapointment, in the East, he had turned his steps again westward, as a second communication from Baltimore indicated hardly a week after the former. In Baltimore he had gone to St. Agnes Hospital for treatment on his carbuncle and had afterwards requested the authorities to get him to the B. & O. Depot for Chicago. Instead, however, they had sent him out to said retreat, conscientiously no doubt - providentially I trust - convinced that he was in no fit condition to be traveling a- lone. Indeed the more we have learned about that institution and the more I've considered his condition both at the time and since, the more too am I convinced that he could hardly landed in a better or a more providential place. At all events we at the Monastery here looked opon his going thither as an answer to prayer and as an evi- dence that he was in God's guidance. Only later on it dawned on my mind that my simple proposition - as said above - to pray, rather than simply read, the "Coronation". But where the connection between reading a book and the obtain- ing of such a favor! Why urge such reading? Why suggest it as a last remedy when everything else seems futle? This might seem quite a question to ask. And as a rule questions are more easily asked than answered. It ought to be selfunderstood that no simple reading of any book is going to move the Heart of Heaven in our favor. Only inasmuch as any book or page can serve to raise the heart to God and thus draw His blessings to us can it be said to have any quality of prayer a- bout it. But besides this, to profit by reading, even the holyist prayers - even about God Himself - the heart of the reader must be disposed. In other words if we want to profit by our reading about God and His saints we must read with reverence. We must appreciate. We speak of the Holy Bible, the Holy Gospel, etc, because the Church has declared them to be inspired writings and because millions have profited from their perusal; have learned to believe in God and to love Him by devoutly reading about him therin. Others have read therin without profit; others again to their own detriment. Why so? How? Failure of disposition; Want of reverence. "unlearned and un- stable wresting the scripture to their own destruction. Now in my opinion, there is hardly another book written out- side the Bible itself, more "inspired-like and more inspiring than this wonderful work, "the Mystical City of God" Its introduction alone , if read with prayerful attention will hardly leave a doubt as to its supernatural origin. The opposition it has met with from the beginning, positively on part of Hell and irreligion is another proof if its worth in the saving of immortal souls. Its emphatic and reiterated approval on the part of Catholic universities, Bishops and Popes in face of said opposition, as well as, its manifest har- mony with Holy Scripture, philosophy & sacred theology - in fact its outstanding preeminence in relation to each and all of these - and its acknowledged crowning and climax in asceticism, ought to remove every honest doubt as to the sincerity and candor as well as the humility of the actual writer, that it is not her own but the work 'of the peerless Mistress of heavenly Wisdom - under divine quidance nothing less than the autobiography of the incomparable Queen of the Universe, Mary conceived without _ Virgin Mother of God.

NOTE: With a tinge of fraternal humor, the following letter -- at once poetic, yet decidedly earnest -- will be found a relief for any color of the "blues" (in season). A missionary in the Philippines, Rev. Edward Casey, writes an elder brother, Rev. Maurice Casey, at the time in Yonkers, N. Y. The latter, having resumed studying after twenty years vacation continued with the younger and was ordained just a year before him. Then after eighteen years of pastoral and missionary work joined the Capuchin Order as Fr. Joachim. The "K" - "C" used as an example, is at the same time familiar to the brothers as an equivalent of Casey.

Alas! however, as dear Father was wont to repeat, the proverb: "Man proposes-God disposes." Poor, dear Maurice's health failed and he came home from the Seminary a family disappointment and worse than that in his own words: "a misfit, a personal failure - - a sadly misfit and personal failure." Ah! It was about that time that silver began to tell its story in Mother's hair and Father's sighs would bring a gentle Soliloquy: "If I had to start life over again, I'd be a priest." . . Winters and summers slipped away. Years and decacs rolled by. Never to be discouraged under such circumstances would surely be more than human. But this was by no means the first knock he had met, and God, if "those whom God loves He tries," it was far from being the last he was to wether. It did not take too long to adjust himself to what seemed next best. He would promote vocations in others at least and in this way possibly in- fluence someone to take his place at the Altar, in the confessional, on the missions. Second of ten brothers in a family of 16, he had started afore- said E'd. F. to the Seminary and after twenty years vacation had served at the First Mass of another younger brother whom also he had helped.

God bless you and yours. I hope you are well and that the silence you maintain is only an indication that your time, like my own, flies, whither I hardly know; so that it seems almost continually blaming me for doing nothing and getting nowhere. There are so many letters, e. g. I ought to write and still so few I get off, as I would like to do personally, and as is often expected. Thanks be to God, however, my health has been good; so that, as a rule 18 hours a day hardly seems to weigh me down at all. Again, "Deo Gratias." We've had hardly any colds in the Monastery this year and very little sickness otherwise. I just hope that we may some day learn to appreciate His graces and be grateful to God. Thanks be to God, we have good word from Father Joachim, as the en- closed copy of his letter will convince you. According to it, you will see that he is figuring on saying Holy Mass again before long. God grant it may come to that soon -- "Deo Volente." I am not sure if I told you before of my dismay at same poor, dear Fr. M. J. 's defection, as it has seemed now close to two years, viz., since his unrest began to show itself threatening. You wrote him at the time yourself, earnest, practical lines of advice. I tried to do so too. Well, months went on before the real break came. What was in his mind, and how it was there, is not easy to say. He had been suffering for quite some time from a fearful carbuncle on the back of his neck - whether a cause or an effect of something else - enough to set many a man crazy. At all events, while the local doctor found nothing positively wrong with his mind, there seemed to be little or nothing to be done for him or with him in the Monastery. They sent him, there- fore, to the hospital in Fond du Lac, Wis., or some other, where his case was believed to be hardening of the brain-arteries or something of that nature. Not knowing him as he ought to be, the authorities of said hospital or hospitals, seemingly made little of his case and let him go for himself. He 'phoned me from Chicago asking to speak to Father Provincial, and, I believe, that was Monday of Holy Week last year. I positively failed to recognize his voice. Next day, our dear friend, Father Coughlin, called me from Royal Oak, whither Father M. J. had come and said Holy Mass. Again, his voice was so strange that even when che swo of the= assured me it was he who was talking, I could not recognize anything like his own voice. Father Provincial sent me out to see what might be done for him, etc., We had dinner together with Father Coughlin and household; after which the three of us had a confidential conference for half an hour or so. -- Fr. C. God bless him, was as practical and as earnest as if he were broadcasting to millions. On his appeal to do so, Mr. M. J. came home to the Monastery and apologized to Father Provincial for any scandal caused; upon which followed a conference that was not too tame or too promising amicable, anyhow. (?) With his letter of "exit, etc.," he took an air-plane to Chi- cago, on his way, as we all presumed, back to Saint Paul, or, as I thought, possibly to the Coast before returning to his docese. How- ever, he seemed so little his real self that my heart was heavy. All I could do was just hope and pray on, as I am sure, poor saint- ly Mother must have felt and done five and fifty years before, when he broke down at the Seminary and came home, etc., You can figure, therefore, on my surprise, when a few days later I received a wire from the very Rev. Rector of St. Mary's Seminary, Baltimore, Mary- land, that Father M. J. had come thither and was not well. He had said Holy Mass once or twice with some difficulty, -- I learned by 'phone that night, and had gone to New York. About a year before that, I had started to read the fourth book of the Mystical City of God. -- "THE CORONATION," -- and, as yet, I was only about half through. You have an idea, I am sure, of how little time I get to read outside the Monastery office. Well, instead of speeding up my efforts to finish the book, I decided to start over again and to read it with due reverence from the beginning. Without a word about it to anyone, I felt that our Blessed Mother would know what I was doing and why. . . . I could hardly help being anxious. I I try not to be. Rather, on the contrary, am trying to foster con- fidence in the wisdom and good ness of God and the powerful inter- cession of our Blessed Mother Mary. "Deo Gratias." Well, a few days later, a telegram from the Monastery on West 31st St., N. Y. - City, to the effect that Fr. wanted to get into St. Elizabth Hospital. What to do? So far, he had failed . Father Provincial had gone to Calvary, Wis., in the meantime, and on reception of the telegram by special delivery, wired the Fr. Guardian in 31st St., to do all in his power to help Father get into St. Elizabeth's or some other like it. Poor Fr. M. J. . . . . however, could not be located . . . . Heart-sick, as I imagine he must have been, at disapointment after disapointment in the East, he had turned his steps again westward. This a second com- munication from Baltimore indicated hardly a week after the former. In Baltimore he had gone to St. Agnes Hospital for treatment on his carbuncle and had afterwards requested the authorities to get him to the B. & O. Depot for Chicago. Instead, however, they had sent him out to said retreat, conscientiously, no doubt - pro- videntially, I trust - convinced that he was in no fit condition to be traveling alone. Indeed, the more we have learned about that in- stitution and the more I've considered his condition, both at the time and since, the more too am I convinced that he could hardly have landed in a better or a more providential place. Deo Gratias At all events, we at the Monastery here looked upon his going thither as an answer to prayer and as nothing less than evidence that he was in God's guidance. Only later, it dawned on my mind that my simple proposition -- as said above -- to pray, rather than simply read the "Coronation" was, possibly, being considered too. But where the connection between reading a book and the obtain- ing of such a favor? Why urge such reading? Why suggest it as a last remedy when everything else seems futile? This might seem quite a question to ask, and, as a rule, questions are more easily asked than answered. It ought to be self understood that no simple reading of any book is going to move the Heart of Heaven in our favor. Only inas- much as any book or page can serve to raise the heart to God and thus draw His blessings to us can it be said to have any quality of prayer about it. But, besides this, to profit by reading, even the holiest prayers - even about God Himself - the heart of the reader must be disposed. In other words, if we want to profit by our reading about God and his saints, we must read with reverence. We must appreciate. We speak of the Holy Bible, the Holy Gospel, etc., because the Church has declared them to be inspired writings and because millions have profited from their perusal; have learned to believe in God and to love Him by devoutly reading about Him therein. Others have read the same holy pages without profit; others again, to their own detriment. Why so? How? Failure of disposition; Want of reverence. "Unlearned and unstable wresting the scriptures to their own destruction. Now, in my opinion, there is hardly another book written outside the Bible itself more "inspired-like and more inspiring than this wonderful work," The Mystical City of God." It's introduction alone, if read with prayful attention will hardly leave a doubt as to it's supernatural origin. The opposition it has met with from the beginning and this at times positively on the part of Hell and irreligion, ought to be another proof of it's worth in the saving of immortal souls. It's emphatic and reitterated approval on the part of Catholic universities, Bishops and Popes in face of such opposition, as well as it's intrinsic value and manifest harmony with Holy Scriptures, philosophy and sacred theology -- in fact, it's outstanding preeminence in relation to each and all of these, and it's acknowledged climax in asceticism, ought to remove every honest doubt as to the sincerity and candor of the actual writer, as well as to the modesty of her claims, that the work is not her own but that of the peerless Mistress of heavenly wisdom -- under divine guidance, nothing less than the autobiography of the incom- parable Queen of the Universe, Mary, conceived without sin, Virgin Mother of God, -- and think of it! - Our Blessed Mother.

God bless you and all. Thanks be to the Good God for all things. His ways like all His works are so deep, so divine. I just read your interesting communication, which for some time I have been more or less expecting - possibly with a tinge of a gentle ear-pull at your not having recently heard / Br'klin. Thank God again for yourself and Fr. Maurice J's good health and for whatever His great plans may materialize for us in the near and distant future - always planning for our best - " .. if we only don't spoil His plans by ours" . Well, I am sure you will be pleased to know that I did finally wake up and take at least some steps toward your seeing Bishop Molloy. I had a very nice little visit with his auxeliary last Friday, Bishop Carney. He seems to be quite a modest, friendly, young Prelate and showed a decided interest in your work for religious schools in the Philippines. I had heard before that it is not too easy to see His Excellency Bishop Molloy and therefore, it did not surprise me when 1 intimated something to that effect. However, he seemed promising and pleased when I suggested that with his coaching us just a little that difficulty could probably be minimized. This especially since he had assured me that he himself is there in the Chancery practically every day. Your coming in May or June therefore would probably be oppor- tune. For that matter he did not make any suggestions when we should come, except that he said he would be away the week of April 11th, since he is expected in Milwaukee for the Consecration of a new Bishop. I did not ask him but I understand its to be Msgr. Meyers - new Bishop of Superior. Yes, my coming hither to St. Michael's has been a decided re- lief to me from the continued drain and strain of difficulties brought to the office for twenty years at St. Bonaventure's in Detroit. I do have perhaps as long hours but its a change. Here its correspondence takes most of my time. There, I simply had to leave most of that to others; and while I meet with pathetic cases to solve or try to aleviate the strain and tension is by no means so pressing. In brief conclusion of this page, I wish you would make a special memento for a couple of problems I have been working on without the progress I'd be encouraged to see. "Better late than never", Answered Joe Ferbush working on the roof of the "new granery" down on the Burkhardt farm when I called him to supper, lamenting tardiness. So, while to have thanked you in the beginning for your charitable interest and faith in the Seraphic Mass Association together with the welfare of our dear ones in estrangement from the ways of peace .... I'll do so now; while, this time at least, I shall prepare certificates according- ly, etc. Hoping that you may, without too much trouble supply my skip- ping and slipping in the course of the above and with best regards and God's blessing to Father Maurice Joachim, Father Klein, and Father Harrington and all our friends you may chance to meet, I hope to remain, of service to you and your good work etc, P.S. Dear Monsignor E'd. I thought it over and have made out the inclosed card .... I figure the poor fellow "got his foot in it ( very likely) without realizing its danger. If you think it advisable to send it to him or should you prefer me to do so, you could return it and give me M M's Ad.

I sure hope you are well. I wrote a card to Fr. M. E. Joachim this morning and it's been on my mind all day that I should send you also a few lines. You can guess about the time if I say that just a year about this time you and I were passing through beautifully picturesque little Sta. Barbara, as nearing Los Angeles. Thanks be to God -- and our dear ones adown the Coast, - was it not quite a privilege, all in all? Some day, D. v., I'll tell you of the rest of my trip after I and poor, dear Owen left you on the bus for Mt. Anges1. Suffice now to say that I arrived in Seattle that p.m. at 6:30 in Spokane, Tuesday at 7:15 a.m. in St. Paul Thurs. 10:30 p.m. on schedule; in Chicago about 6:30 p.m. Friday: Detroit Sat. at 4:30 p.m. Convent Mass next a.m .; New York and Brooklyn Monday a.m. and p.m. respectively. From Los Angeles Only missed two holy Masses, Deo gratias. Well, you burried the mortal remains of poor dear . Gus - Austin rather, since he prefered and as I told him, so much more like the real name of the great doctor of the Church. I would like to have details of his last days. He wrote me quite a touching letter from the hospital apparently after his first operation, seemingly quite cool and philosophical about what might come -- and certainly with beautiful faith. He evidently knew that he had cancer. Just a few of his words: "I have observed that very seldom is cancer cured ... at least by surgery. "I am relying on the Sacred Heart to come to my rescue . " . .. "I was privileged to receive our Lord at 6 a.m. the morning they opened me; and again on the 2nd day (1st Friday) , Thanks and praise to the Sacred Heart." How beautifully condescending that the Merciful Sacred H't actually did come to his rescue on His own blessed Feast! He had written me a number of times to pray for Pat., even before he was sick. I am sure he was praying for his -- their reconsiliation, etc. and how beautifully did it not come about! How grateful we ought to be that we can confidently hope that we have another, another of our original sixteen -- with dear Father and Mother -- waving us from beyond the grave to follow their footsteps in keeping the faith, in praying for one another as among the INTERESTS OF THE SACRED HEART and striving manfully against the world, the flesh and the devil for the one great prize of the final BEATIFIC VISION. Mary Ann was the first to cross the border into eternity and saintly little Martha a week later -- innocent children -- and the others following after, judging from their patience in their final struggles and the seemingly brightness of their faith in God, give great hope that so far every one of them have made the Great Grade, have saved their souls -- the one thing necessary -- and with so many of our dear ones of kin and neighbors are praying for us and asking our prayers. Ah !.. What else is this than just a little side-view of the great Communion of the Saints? Thanks and praises and Glory be to God! I just felt I'd have to bring the note I meant to start, on evening of the 4th to an end. I hope it has not bored you. The inclosed letter from Miss Ryan in New York will give an idea of what my hopes were -- still are -- of converting our wayward family and clan to seraphic love of God and our Bl. Mother Mary, by having them read and pray the wonderful, all-outstanding "Autobiography of God's eternally chosen Queen of the Universe", the "Mystical City of God". Dear Edward: I think Miss Ryan would appreciate a line from you, of appreciation and of encouragement. Better a verse. She had been quite a successful business-lady before the War. I think it was in 1942 that quite an unexpected order came from Washington to "scrap" all prints and cuts not in actual use unless redeemed, etc. The redemption-fee on the Mystical City of God prints was quite an item; $500.00 I believe; and with a bishop in whose jurisdiction these prints were stored forbidding the rescue, it certainly looked dark for them. However, Miss R. who seems to be specially devoted to the Holy Ghost ... came spontenously to the rescue delighted that she was able to do so and thanking God that the prelate's prohibition had come too late. Her business, as predicted by the publisher at the time has tribled since. She is probably in her fortys now. Hoping to go more exclusively into the business of saving souls, she is now figuering on disposing of her property and material affairs. So make a memento for her holy guidance now and then at least .... Love to all in the west and to dear Fr. M. E. J. when you get back to St. Paul. Fr.Sol. ut supra.

The above was written by the present Rt. Rev. Msgr. E'd F. Casey to his youngest brother, whom he had preceeded by birth about fifteen months, Father M. J., about whom the writer is concer ned, is their second eldest brother -- now the eldest living. Owen was the youngest of ten brothers with three sister among his nine brothers ahead of him and three more immediately following. These three are still living -- now grandmas. The writer briefly touches on dear Mother's beautiful death. May she rest with saints in Heaven. Thanks be to God for the great grace He provided her, for the ten-day fearful, yet glorious struggle, that preceeded her wonderful victory in a Happy Death P. S. The writer of the above, Rt. Rev. Edw'd, was rescued from the Jap. Prison Los Bonos. with two bishops, 150 priest and one hundred twenty-five nuns among over 2000 prisoners. Very early the morning of February 23rd, 1943 the day on which the desperate Japps would seem to have been planing a whole-sale masacre of them; they were rescued by the MacArthur Forces. Father Maurice was nicely able and went to the First Holy Mass Celebration of our Jesuite Nephew, John Mccluskey the following June 24th and has been saying holy ever since. Thanks be to God.

Hoping that my tardiness in answering your letters early in December may not scandalize, I am trying these few days to makd up for lost time - three in-a-row. I hoped to get one of those "Begone S." I know I had a couple of them in Brooklyn, but whether or not they put them in or if I can find them now among other things I am not certain. Till shortly before Christmas I was continually getting behind in my correspondence; though others helped me now and then. Now, thank God Fr.Michael, one of my former altar boys from Pitt Street I. Y. and now one of our missionaries helps me when not away. However, I am going to try and get a copy of that booklet for you. I must have one somewhere I am trying to get this off Air-special so as if possible to overtake the one I mailed you yesterday without name of comment regular mail. As to that $20. check, of Dec. 10th: not knowing what you might want me to do with it, I am enroling the Poor Holy Souls for your intion. - at least till further instructed, - i.e. 310. of it. P.S. Remind me again of the booklet please. It is out of print, otherwise, too bad.

I hope this finds you in the best of health and hopes. Thanks be to God we are quite well down here in St. Felix. After a cold and wet spring -- even black frost on the 8th the weather has turned quite ideal. Deo Gr. I was certainly pleased to receive a very bright letter from Fr. M. Joachim last week, about the best in a long time. It really looks like his old self once more. Thanks be to God "a billion." I wrote him several weeks ago that I had already permis - sion to go on a trip to Chicago and St. Paul, etc. at my choice and leaving the arrangements to yourself and him. I believe he said he sent you a copy of said letter. Well, We expect V. Rev. Fr. Provincial down from Detroit shortly -- just back from Guam and several other islands in the Pacific, and I anticipate no difficulty in obtaining permission to go also to Superior as M. J. proposes. I would be glad to have any suggestions that might heighten interests relative to the proposition. I'll probably get a week or so off for the trip. So I'll be more or less depending on your arrangements for a program, etc. I have not heard just lately from any one in the farther west. Please God it's indicative of smoothe sailing out that way. Thanks be to God and our Bl. Mother Mary and all the Communion of Saints. P. S. I believe I owe you a couple letters since January. The trouble is -- too often -- I put letters aside till I can answer them properly and the 1st thing I know they're snowed under and often forgotten. Please pardon.

Rev. Fr. Guardian, after a little consultation just noted -- tentatively -- that I could start June 1st or 2nd. Of course I think that would be rather early, unless there were a purpose for it. If we had a mission to do somewhere before the anniversary or possibly preferably after, we could arrange accordingly. They are having a meeting in Saint Bonaventure's these three or four days, of the Definitorium and I understand that right thereafter Father Provincial after many thousand miles travel is figuring on coming down here for a rest. -- a sort of private retreat for himself I presume. There is a possibility that I be sent back there to Detroit or elsewhere, though I hardly think it at all probable. I have not the least worry about whether I re- main here or be transferred. It is after all, essentially quite the same. It is such a surpassing privilege to know definitely that one is doing God's holy will by keeping the rule and obeying. Sorry to say, if we can use the word, it is so little possible for any of us to appreciate such privileges. Indeed, just herein seems to me to be humanity's great weakness, WANT OF APPRECIATION. But again how fortunate for us that God's mercy is above all His works -- and His patience is essentially one with His mercy.

God bless you and yours. Pardon my tardiness in complying with demands of -- correspondence. Thanks be to God I've had some really practical exercises recently that befit a capuchin novitiate ..... Four weeks ago we drove over to Milwaukee for a celebration in honor of Fr. Stephen Eckert, whose Dominicad (Dominican brother) Br. Michael you must have .... . From Notre Dame .... Afterwards they ambulanced me to St. Michael's Hospital - thence after two days to St. Felix - St. Joseph Hospital Ft. Wayne for two long weeks (16 days) and now again back to the Novitiate .... Deo Gratias. They seem to think they had pretty critical patient I can genuflect again .... and can eat - "no foolin." Now to catch up a little with letters, etc .... God help us ... I surely sympathize with you and your practical associate .. . . Best wishes to all ...... including down to the personnel of St. Joseph Hospital where I met such really fraternal and sister- like encouragement !.... I always bring away with me newly awakened memories from St. Thomas. God bless Fr. Cashman ... and all the great work:

God bless you and yours -- Aye and -- including this poor plodder. I surely hope you keep well. Thanks be to God we are well down here. We've had a very mild Winter, hardly any snow to speak of and practically no colds. All this, not- withstanding quite a lot of rain and early in the week a visita- tion of sleet and freezing rain that in quite a few places shrubs and trees were loaded down to breaking down. The inclosed telegram came the night before last and Grace phoned yesterday morning giving more particulars and asking that I let you know about the situation. Bernard, Sr. had been out on some official busines in Eureka, was quite occupied Thursday evening so that he neglected some kind of a natural call to which he was not as promptly obedient as Grandmother Nature often has to insist on. So he had to go to the hospital for treatment. Grace did not seem to think it very serious coparatively. We hope of course that it was not serious. However, they are right -- we do right rather -- to pray that nothing serious come of such experiences. Otherwise every one seems to be holding their own on the Coast. How can we ever be thankful as we ought to be! Glory be to God. Inclosed is also a letter from poor, dear Brother Pat. He too seems well and, glad to see, still retains a coloring of favorable humor. I should have had this off yesterday morning, as I told Grace I would and by all means meant to do. ... Please pardon.

I just read the photo you sent me of our dear Father M. E. Joachim's tomb-marker and, sitting here with my two feet on another chair am using it as a writing desk. Deo gratias. I've not said holy Mass since last Thursday. The skin-burns I wrote you about last week (if it got off), started the eczema activity again - after I'd had a Dr. Stan Casey treat the former. He sent me to a skin- specialist in Ft. Wayne, Dr. McNairy, who stresses with treatment, "feet up." I would have offered holy Mass yesterday but Fr. Guardian thought better keep to Dr.'s orders. So that will probably mean a week or so before I'm on my feet again properly. Thanks be to God is gives me comparatively little pain or itch; so that time does not hang so painfully as it might otherwise. As for above-said "marker", I think we should be grateful indeed that the good God enabled us to procure such a creditable "memorial. Extremely brief of course, but even so, who knows how many a vocation its simple reading may be destined to awaken, to encourage, to anchor. Ah ! "Its simple reading' ? ~ and the prayers and sighs there offered for vocations and, as we may surely hope, reinforced and reechced in Purgatory or and indeed even in Heaven - Fr. M. E. J. still active. Comparatively very few ever tried to fathom the meaning of those twenty years of humiliation to Fr. Maurice. And still fewer I think ever knew of the, at-least-dozen-yrs dispointment and humiliations where- by she merciful Divine Wisdom deigned to chisel and to emery him down to such calmly perfect acceptance of God's holy designs - as manifested both in the Mt. Hope San. and especially as you were privileged to see him, during rosary, slumber into Eternity; -- the "change", the transition -- "Tuis enim fidelibus Domine Vita Mutatur non taliture." .. Oremus pro invicem ...

Dec. 26 - God bless you Father E'd - Rt. Rev Msg. rather. I meant to reach you before the beautiful Feast Xmas as indeed was on my mind in regards to quite some others. Br. Owen is about to start back for the West - been here Monday night. He seems to hold his own, Deo Gr. - back to Chicago first. Thanks be to God We've all been well here at the St. Felix lately. with few exceptions. Now O. B. J. (Owen) comes along and is about to seal his letter. So suggests that I just put it in with his. . . I did hope to have you call on your return or your return from your missions in New York. Thank God for the success. ·

P. S. ? Perhaps rather a new start for above May 2nd. It was not without surprise that I found the foregoing card in the machine when I went with this to start my "Te Deum, (afterwards inserting the "10:15 P. M., etc.) Incidently, I was probably more surprised than disapoin- at not going to Milwaukee. Thank the Lord, I was able to smile at the profference of both. The Vice-Postulator of the cause, V. Rev. Nerius, O. M. Cap. probably found the time too short before start- ing off for Europe and Rome to hold another conference. There is to be a General Chapter in Rome - starting with a triduum of prayer to the Holy Ghost on the 18th for God's holy Grace and guidance. Of course we'd all like to see Fr. Clement of Milwauke retained, D. v. - excepting Fr. Clement himself who has already sent some of baggage back ahead of him to U. S. . . He is known to be rather of a retiring disposition - from responsabilities. Many thanks for your interesting letter last week. I got a mes- I hope it may in some way break sage of yesterday to Jimmy Ryan. the ice for what we hope the holy Ghost may deign to promp you to do. Jimmy must be now about 80. He was next to Kate . I rec- eived a very interesting letter from Br. Pat yesterday. . Quite busy and hopeful. Thank be to God. Mildred Conley phoned a few minutes ago from Chicago quite some details about Neil and Gene- vieve's going to Europe.

God Bless us all - Yourself and myself and all our friends and honest enemies if such there be. More than six weeks ago, having readyour letter I started to respond at once . . . God help us! I just got started and here we have Sexigesima. Thanks be to God! though we've had quite a little grippe-weather the last three months, we so far, have had but one case of that epidemic. Up in Detroit since Wednesday, I just returned . . finding 3 full sets of the Mystical City of God in our Cell (% Wallace Bedolfe who was here over night about a week ago) Miss Doris Panyard of 1705 Peck Street Muskegan, Michigan just phoned me that he requested four sets -- one for himself. Deo gratias! -- a promising 23 yr. oldster who was baptised as was his elder Br. Bob and Sister Barbara. No doubt Grace has told you about them Air View. St. Felix Friary - Victory Noll overlooking the Wabash in distant rear --- left. Headq's of the Missionary Catechists. We think this snapped by a local Minister who is said to have a hobby in such.

My dear Brother Edward. Rt. Rev. Monsignore: God bless you these days of grace. I started Monday with the intention of writing you a letter as I hoped would be worthwhile. I have not been able to finish it and my answer to your proposition about the Gregorian Masses ought to be already on the way thither. In a way I regret I'll have to be a disappointment in this really generous proposition You will understand from the fact that as members of the Order we have as a rule only the disposal of two holy Mass intentions per month. Otherwise all intentions for holy Masses are life (left) to the disposal and appointment of the local Superior. I have enrolled poor, dear Grace, however, anumber of times in the Seraphic Mass -Association, which in my conviction, means, each time an emmense benefit. In fact, judging from the reports of favors as received there therefrem, it is not easy to find a comparason. Deo gratias! Some how I did not receive word of Grace's death till after my High-Mass on Sunday April 12. Some one phoned about it while I was on the Altar saying they would call later and that was the end of it. Brother Porter was not particular about the name of the caller but Thomas Brady wired that evening. Luckyly someone had sent in a request for a special holy Mass for Fr. Sol's Intent., and the following day I had a regular Missam propriam. I was happy to offer them both for poor, dear, Grace Agatha R. I. P. After all, how can we ever be grateful as we ought to be, for another so hopeful and beautiful death added to the happy list so far without exception. Glory and thanks be to God! Re - quiescant I.P. It would just seem that dear Mother and Father are keeping up their happy old night-prayers for -- "and for a happy death and a favorable judgement." I hope we all -- still left behind in this exile -- keep up on our part too that beautiful so beautiful feature of Communion of Saints. God bless you again Father - -

I want to reach you with this as soon as possible so that it be convenient for you to profit by a little proposition - up my sleeve since your interesting let- ter from White Plains, in reference to your betsg plans to be in the Green Bay Diocese during August. You probably remember me telling you about Mr. Philip Obrien of Chicago - just now on his summer-far ?if- teen miles out of Bailey's Harbor, Wisconsin, I called his amiable Wife Eleanor last nite - a little like Mrs. Tom Tobin of fifty years ago. ... They were expecting you to call on them earlier in the Summer before they left Chicago. Now they will be expecting you to get in touch with them and to stay with them at least a few days before the Month slips by. Their telephone - please don't disapoint us, then & - is: 15 R. 34. Waseda Farm Bailey's Harbor, Wisconsin. "3€ sure and have him reverse charges. We will see to his coming." P.M. Well, I did miss this a.m.'s pick-up, but I hope to reach you soon enough to make it conveni- ent for you/ see them in the near future. In a way I am confident that it will be close at least to as good as a "parish apointment," I shall try to reach them with a letter ahead of you. . Barbara Bedolfe phoned, and Wallace himself wrote about his first confession and Holy Communion two weeks ago. Deo Gr! I believe it was on August 2nd.

Congratulations on your practical Write in the "Priest." Too bad you could'nt have it in a hundred publications. Miss Beatrice McCahill was over from Chicago, 7612 N. Ashland. She promised a $100 for your Seminary some time ago if she got a certain favor. . Here with you'll find same. Delighted to give the surprise. I am trying to get it off To-Day. God help us! I hardly seem to be getting anything done - any- yet so much to be done. I am often at my wits' end what to do first. · God bless us all.

I hope this finds you well. I've not been too well now for a good week. But thank God I've been able to say holy Mass. We hope to see the Crisi in the Mercy Hall Hospital case, Detroit very soon. Her Enemies have hesitated at nothing to put over their lies.

God bless you My Dear Rt. Rev. Brother Edward. God bless you and yours these unsettled days - at once - days of threatening forebodings and of manifestations of God's/Wisdom and Power merciful Goodness without end or & limit; the former on the part of irrelition and worldly-inclined humanity. And God help us! Who can presume to claim exemption from that stupid in- clination? . .. Hence too, our natural tendency to listen to even vain forebodings and to fear for ourselves personally as well as for crazy - be- cause sinful - humanity in general? Incidently, it was about twelve years ago that a certain (Jewish) Rabbi Rosenwasser came the Office here in the St. Bonaventure Monastery, lamenting the prevalence of atheism - most especially he stressed; " ... among the rising Jewish generation". Fr. S. politely invited him into an instruction room. Then, without a word on a piece of tissue-paper - the Rev. Rabbi's index (Unfinished Draft) NOTE: This informal. . . came a few days after the happy death of our dear Sister, Mrs. Grace Brady, last Easter Friday, 4/10/53. Her real struggling had started sometime before, her dear husband's death, which occured more than a year earlier. Hers - stomach cancer. P.S. The verses were written while he was still in college and as yet she was still dreaming of going to the convent. She left three sons, a daughter and about ten grand children.

Thanks be to God! In receiving no news yesterday -- from Margaret and Frank, we were confirmed in our confidence and in God that He would surprise the doctors in regard to her threatening carcinoma operation. I hope that all her friends may -- grateful to God offer a few holy communions in earnest thanksgiving. How wonder -- in all His designs with all who confide in Him. How fortunite! -- How humbly grateful we ought to be! Deo Gratias! A Million! Thanks be to God, though comparatively unnoted and quiet God granted us the gracious privilege to celebrate a happy diamond jubilee in the Order and in the holy habit if Saint Frances. This took place Monday, January 14, at solemn high Mass. I would hardly know how it could have been more beautiful, under the simple circumstances. ... I had come to the holy novitiate Christmas Eve. and six months ahead of the seven other students who joined me the following July. They are all gone on to Heaven now, we hope, with their senior of all, Father Damasus, in his 90th year . Had he waited five months longer he and I would have had golden jubilee together. He was patient and joyful to the last. May he be privileged to await in the peace of the saints, the inconceivable glory of the Gen. Ressurection. Pl. pardon the digresxion: To-day Deo Gratias, it is sixty years and sixty days I was invested. It was probably my fault that the cdldbfzgion (celebration)

It is nearly time for office - Matins - Lauds - I want to answer the above Tonight if I can I perhaps should have told the secret before - of having prayers heard in "hopeless cases." Any how I think a few little notes near by will be interestingly Encouring - over. I had to cross proposed P.S. off. - can only hope to do something better than just a P.S. Another letter from same niece Clement informs of the operation - Let us continue praying and trusting and thanking - God first of course and then all else Since the novices are gone I've been having - so far - the privilege of serving Fr. Rudolph's Mass every morning. . I really enjoy it but - but - One hardly knows how to get around . ·

God bless you and all yours -- and sure including my poor self in every blessing I can get or give. Thanks be to God for the Faith and for all His blessings. I had Fr. Edward with me at the Monastary nearly 2 months to June 18th. Back from the Philippines, as you know, he was doing real missionary work for religion in the "Far East" something over the 12 months he was here. He seemed to enjoy his stay at St. Bonaventure's. I certainly did. Shortly after leaving Detroit and back to his headquarters in St. Paul, he received information from his Bishop in the Philippines that he is expected back there in September. It is possible that he may not be able to get this way again before his voyage west- ward. Musing together over the celebration of his Jubilee, and the triple vacation it occasioned us, we agreed that it were theme enough for a little treatise of some kind, whereby to praise the wonderful ways of God's providence, and at the same time, offer an expression of appreciation to the many dear ones -- old and new -- and for the gratitude we all experienced at so many manifestations of kindness at their hands. Details of preparations for that celebration, at least the more remote, will hardly be necessary or expected here. As the Senior of the family -- since dear Ella passed away -- you know those details; having watched the career of each of us longer and perhaps with more interest than anyone else breathing to- day. Something the same might be said also to poor, dear Brother Pat, and, for that matter, though of course with shorter scope of vision back to earlier spring-time of life, to each of the others -- Guss and Owen, and the one-time three little sisters -- now we might say Grandmas -- Margaret, Grace and Mayme. I am not certain if I ever wrote you of Fr. Maurice Joachim's Jubilee in New York. It was suppose to take place just a year ahead of Fr . Edward's. Anyhow, they sent me thither to help him celebrate and, Thank God, we had a very pleasant celebration of about a week or ten days. Thanks be to God. It was about 12 years since my 20 year sojourn in the Empire State, and Fr. M. J. had, in about 7 years, made quite some friends in the same three stations where I had been located ahead of him. A number of our cousins from Boston and elsewhere, including two nuns, attended the solemn Mass as the climax of the celebration, which, Thank God, "went off without a hitch." The following days we visited our different houses in the East, and besides some friends in N. J. Shortly after that celebration the Fathers of our Province held a chapter or convention, for election of new superiors and other affairs of the Province. Such chapters, as a rule, are held every 3 years, and everyone is supposed to be ready for a change, if such come. Fortunately, it seemed to me, and providen- tially, Fr. M. Joachim on this occasion was transferred to one of our largest monastaries, i. e., that of St. Anthony at Marathon, Wisconsin. Before going thither, however, he got permission to take a week or so vacation to visit old friends and places -- notably, in Prescott where we two were born, and "Big River," where we first went to Holy Mass, and to catechism classes, viz., in dear old St. Mary's. Thanks be to God! What colorful memories the mention of these places must awaken in you! They do in me at least and sure you were six when I was born. What a world of experience that meant in advance of the baby !... At all events, Fr. Maurice wrote me shortly after his arrival at St. Antos, of the coming Diamond Jubilee in Prescott, where we were born and baptized, etc., and of a probably invitation that we should attend. Up to this, we had hardly dreamed of Fr. Edward's coming back from the Islands for his Jubilee the following June. Only several months later when the excitement of the Eucharistic Congress at Manila was over, did we learn of his coming. In fact, it was only when he was nearing our shores, in May, that I learned of his actual coming. Not long afterwards, the Pastor of St. Joseph's, in Prescott, not only invited us to the said Jubilee, but about as much as appointed me to give the Jubilee sermon; informing me at the same time that Fr. Edward was to be the Celebrant. Of course I thanked him for the privilege, because, while I never long to go back to any old place from which Divine Providence has seen good to remove me, yet I must acknowledge that I have a natural inclination that way -- like the Israelites in the desert naturally yearned (many of them) to go back to Egypt. No doubt, we are all naturally that way 1 inclined. Probably you remember when, at the Golden Wedding in 1913 we were all musing over scenes and events on the River Bank and in old Trimbelle someone remarked: "Wouldn't it be nice if we could go back there again!", dear Mother, gently sighing as if revisioning the trials of those days, outweighing the beauties and pleasures -- half whispered an exclamation: "Thanks be to God, I'm glad it's over !" Many a time since I've thought: How beautiful was that little exclamation, how really Christian! For my part, I usually con- sole myself and overcome such "hunger of the heart for days and dreamings never more to be," by thinking of the lonesome changes that were already taking place before we left those scenes of our childhood -- scenes of the "burned hills", of the "Big Ravine," of the prairie-fires, etc; and of the "little Poplars", so bright, so beautiful in Spring, and during the day, yet so lonely in the evening; where you, on your way home on a certain evening, (must have been almost night), met a lynx, as you concluded afterwards it must have been, and before you were really scared, must have bluffed it, when, taking it for me, you called out: "Is that you Barney?" Of course, neither of us answered, except, on its part, which was perhaps the best answer we could give under the circum- stances, when it leaped into the ticket and let Jimmy Casey pass. It is not hard to reckon the amount of grass that grew, or that didn't grow, under his feet till Jimmy was over the hill and home over big and little hollows. You must have been about 13 at the time. Pardon for such a digression. I'll never get started. Than too, and this belongs to the same digression, I think of how short in comparison with eternal rewards are the pleasures, as well as the trials of this "exile." After all, what do they either or all amount to, except inasmuch as they buoy us up till the Merciful Father calls us Home, or wean us from inordinate love of the world, and of our- selves -- from deceptions so common this side of Heaven. walked in the world with the worldly", writes Fr. Ryan in his "Son of the Mystic", indicating something of the vanity of figuring on real peace of soul except in God's service and fostering confidence in Him: "I walked in the world with the worldly, I craved what the world never gave.
