And I said: In the world each ideal that sines like a star on life's wave is wrecked on the shores of the real and sleeps like a dream in a grave." Quite in the same spirit too, Moor beautifully tunes in: "Poor wanderers of a stormy day, from wave to wave we're driven; And fancy's flash and reason's ray serve but to light the troubled way ; -- There's nothing calm but Heaven. " Well to get started at last: I left St. Bonaventure's Monastery, Detroit, August 11th, planning to catch the first train to Chi- cago, thence to Marathon, Wis. same day, where I'd meet Fr. Maurice and go with him next day to St. Paul where Fr. Edward was expecting us. I was in time for the train o.k. but for- tunately failed to catch it. The Dear Lord had planned other- wise: though at the time it did seem to me as the result of nothing less than stupidity on my part. It was only three weeks later, having been to Marathon for the first time, I realized that missing the train that morning saved me twice 65 miles on starting out. Altogether it saved me about 300 miles and, as if all prearranged, enabled me to make happy and unexpected con- nections which I would hardly have found possible to make other - wise. Thanks be to God! Instead of to Marathon, I went to Milwaukee, after a very pleasant little repast in Chicago with an old friend, John Gorman and family, who met me at the depot and insisted on us going to a nearby hotel and having dinner. I had not felt particularly hungry at all -- in fact I'd not thought of eating -- but found that close to 12 hours on a cup of coffee and a small slice of bread had provided quite a vacancy when we sat down to a well spread table. How mindful of my need was the Good God to inspire my friend so charitably! We had a real friendly recreation that night in the first monastery (S. Francis) I had visited 40 years before, on my way to the privileged Noviciate. After Holy Mass next morning I got in touch by long distance telephone with Fr. Maurice -- Joachim rather -- and had an under - standing with him to join me at New Lisbon (Wis.) on the west- bound Hiawatha. That gave me till 2 P.M. to visit our different houses in Milwaukee and meet all the Brethern, instead of hurrying away on the Omaha at 10 A. M. At about 4 o'clock we made our second stop at said New L. where Fr. M. J. had arrived by bus from Marathon 65 miles to the north. At Milwaukee a friendly looking priest had boarded the train immediately ahead of me. He had been out to the Mother-house near St. Francis Seminary and, as I learned later, was bringing a whole staff of teaching nuns to take charge of his school some place in Minnesota -- about 20 of them it seemed to me. Besides this there were several other religious. Till we were pulling out of New Lisbon I had felt in doubt as to whether or no they'd been taking me for a venerable rabbi, or for something else more or less ideal. The coach was well filled, and the beard I carried -- had carried more than 40 years -- made me no doubt, at least a little conspicuous. Well, if there had been any misgivings in that direction, Fr. M. Joachim positively settled it with one happy exclamation. As we entered through the vestibule, each with a grip, he stopped as in astonishment and in a clear voice that everyone seemed expecting from one of the gray-beards, called out: "Glory be to God! Look at all the sisters." Crossing the Mississippi (at LaCrosse) , shortly after, said friendly looking priest was calling attention to beauties down the River when I called to him in a half whisper: "Father ; Look upstream. " With that, he seemed to forget the scenery altogether and, coming up to our front seat offered me his hand, asking: "Are you not Fr. Maurice Casey?" "Why!" I answered, as Fr. M. J.'s hand raised to meet his, "This is Father Maurice." All attention seemed on the two of them. They had studied together 30 years before and had not met since ordination. Before we knew it, we were speeding up the Minnesota side on through Redwing, where in 1880 Father Solanus saw railroad cars the first time, and Hastings, where Mother worked as a girl, till across and around the beautiful widening in the River, we watched the great red sun dip to the hills while we glided toward St. Paul and into the Union Depot. Here we met Fr. Edward -- first time since his return from the Philippines. We phoned to your boy-friend of 60 years ago, Mike Costello, and my bed-fellow 10 years later when I was a "roust-a-bout" and he a boiler-maker in the Stillwater Penitentiary. Our dormitory, however, was outside the walls, so we had a "pull" of some kind. Mike is now a sergeant on the St. Paul Police Force. Your Mildred had arranged with her friends, the Conley family, to give us (as indeed they did together with herself) an ideally pleasant little reception. She had a decidedly- choice little surprise "up her sleeve," when, after supper, she brought you to us from Seattle on the "long distance", and we all talked with yourself and Pat, and Emma and Guss -- on my part the first time since the Golden Wedding twenty-five years before. We found ideal quarters in the College of St. Thomas, where Fr. Edward had been Rector before his resignation prior to going to Australia and the Philippines. We made some calls next day after Holy Mass and Breakfast -- Fr. M. J. and I serving each other in turn at the Convent -- and about 2 P.M. left via Sault Ste. Marie to reach Superior about 5:30 -6 o'clock. To our pleasant surprise, whom did we meet at the depot but our old friend Ed Sampson, and his wife, waiting to convey us to the Parish House on 12th and John Sts. She had phoned me a day or two before I left Detroit that they were starting off on their vacation and possibly would see us in Superior. The celebration next day, Feast of the Assumption, was a happy one. Fr. M. Joachim and I having offered our Holy Masses earlier, were ready as deacon and sub-deacon, to assist Fr. Edward at the Solemnity proper. The Rt. Rev. Bishop Reverman attended in state, and Fr. Weber (now Rt. Rev. Msgr.) gave the sermon. The latter is now Vicar General and looks very well. Thanks be to God, everything went off smoothly, both at the Jubilee Mass itself, and at the receptions. The first of these took place immediately after the solemnity in church, when quite a procession of friends came to the school-hall to greet the Celebrant and his Reverend Brothers. The other con- sisted of a gathering of about fifty or more friends for dinner, and a program in a hotel down on Tower Ave. Besides a goodly number of Fr. Edward's class-mates from Sacred Heart School, a number of our cousins and other relatives and old friends from Burkhardt, Detroit, etc. attended. We made quite a number of visits -- taking altogether -- that evening, next day and Tuesday. These visits, though not exactly canonical had more or less the nature of missionary work. Monday A. M. Fr. Joachim and I served each other's Masses in St. Joseph's Convent, down near the East end. What a change in 50 years! They wondered when I told them that I used to carry them on the trolley-cars as they went daily back and forth to school -- only two or three in the whole community. Now they must number about thirty in that Convent, as seemed to me. One of them present remembered those pioneer days. To another, now an invalid seemingly just waiting to take off for Heaven I had the privilege of giving Holy Communion. Deo Gratias. That P. M. we went to bless a little ten year old grand- daughter of Teacher Aggie Murphy Oteir in the "Steel Plant", and some others. I was surprised at the seemingly little change in her appearance in twenty-six years, when she attended Fr. M. Joachim's first Holy Mass. Thence we crossed over St. Louis River to Duluth where we found some old friends from Hudson. Tuesday was short and busy, from the fact that we were to leave for St. Paul about 2 P.m. We arrived via St. Cloud and Minneapolis about 5:30-6 P.m. It was an up-to-date train. Aug. 19th, Thursday, we went over to Stillwater and visited St. Michael's Church, School and Convent. Things are kept in excellent condition. Dear old St. Michael's! The surroundings and views from familiar vantage points are perhaps as beautiful to the younger generation as they were to me fifty or sixty years ago; but to me! Only in the beautiful old Church itself, seemingly unchanged, could I have lingered longer. We sped down Third Avenue and steep Chestnut St., where in 1887 I learned to run the trolley-cars. At the foot of Chestnut, as of old, we crossed on the new bridge, now without toll or a draw and perhaps ten feet higher than was the old draw-bridge. Going down through Wisconsin scenery that still seemed familiar, we had dinner and a congenial visit with Monsignor Owens, who was ordained just a year ahead of Fr. Maurice J. and Master of Ceremonies at his First Holy Mass. We found him, however, in bad shape with some kind of rheumatism. Afterwards we speeded out the old road so familiar in younger, to church-going days to Burkhardt, Boardman and New Richmond. The others waited under the maples for our first stop while Fr. Edward and I climbed the old entrance to the Roberts Estate. We found, I'm inclined to say, poor little Emma, so modest and winsome in school-days and later when Fr. S. helped her Father with the Spring work. She seemed quite alone though gently con- tented and friendly, but of course a little more now than fif- teen. The older of the two, Anna, perhaps more ambitious, married and became a venerated grandma. One of her four sons, I believe, became a professor at Cornell. Her husband died a few years since and the last I heard the two were again together on the farm. Next stop was at the Diehl-Germain home. They, too, were surprised. Anna is the old lady now, and Joe, the old man, quite literally. Thence down across the old bridge and over to Fr. Edward's childhood chum, William Ryan, and wife Agnes, living in Andy Tobin's old house. Leaving the others there, Fr. S. hiked over to Baker's and after a short visit with the dear old lady and Mary, strolled down to the one-time beauti- ful Drydam. In the meantime, the others came and took a longer hike. The old mill at Burkhardt would seem to have been shell shocked or something like that. It has not moved since the war No. 1 and seems to impart a sort of spirit of its own to the whole vicinity. Mrs. Baker seems to hold her own remarkably well. I think she is close to 85. Mary, like the rest of us, has lost her child-like and youthful brightness, but still retains a hopeful and friendly smile. Poor dear Alice was quite ill at the time of our visit. We each gave her our blessing and started for New Richmond, where we had a congenial visit with Andy Tobin and family. Leaving there after supper, we stopped to see Anna Ryan and her brother John, just outside the city toward Boardman. Her we found Scott Tobin, my one-time boy- friend, and wife Jane (Henry) . Thence we sped back to Monsignor Owens to offer Holy Mass next day -- Feast of my dear Patron St. Bernard. Our chauffeur and associate whom Sister Mary Kathleen (Doonan) had sent us for the whole day, went on to St. Paul and the Orphanage. God bless them all. I had the privilege once more of offering the Holy Sacrifice where for the first time I had attended a solemn Mass -- three priests -- and that at Midnight. It was Christmas Eve in 1881 when with Ryans' roadsters and our new sleighs a real load of us started in the ten miles when it was 18 below zero, and before we got home it was 22 below. The ceremonies were beautifully inspiring. Thanks be to God! They have a fine school now where in 1886 or 1887 Papa and Maurice and Mr. Ryan, Matt and Peter Welsh and young Jim Pachingham broke ground for dear Fr. Kelly. How happy he was, insisting that we come down to Reilly's and have a good dinner. Tears of appreciation filled his eyes, more expressive than any words he could have uttered. Later in the morning we went for a hike, climbing the bluff to the south whence is a surprisingly beautiful view, not only of the city itself and the St. Croix River, but of Stillwater and the new State Prison layout, with Mt. St. Helen in the distance to the right. I gradually recognized the hill on which we stood as one I had dreamed about, off and on, ever since I had left Yonkers, without knowing what it could all mean. It is quite park-like on top with a single grave and a flagpole, etc. We said the rosary together for the living and the dead as we peered down where it would be dangerous to des - cend, and went down the West side. On our return to the Rectory, we found Fr. Owens -- Pardon! Rt. Rev. Monsignor -- where he'd been most of the time for some weeks with rheumatism sitting with two helpless feet on a chair in front of him. We each blessed them in turn, someone remarking that a triple blessing ought to help some way. Well, Thanks be to God, he seemed better as he came to dinner with us and, afterwards, put on his shoes and "shot us over" to St. Paul. Next evening (Saturday) , Dean Conley brought us via Hudson and River Falls to Prescott, where we met some old friends who took us to the Rectory, where they were preparing for the Jubilee celebration next day. The Rev. Pastor from St. Mary's, Big River, met us there and took Fr. M. J. and myself out with him to offer Holy Mass next morning. Fr. Maurice said the first Mass -- 6:30, and gave a touching little sermon. The attendance was good, and quite a few Holy Communions. The same old St. Mary's, beautiful and well kept as ever, has been built out on both sides since we were there sixty years back, so that it would nicely accommodate probably eight hun- dred. The Rev. Pastor came back from his mission and in a very short time we were in Prescott, vesting for the Solemn Mass, His Excellency, Bishop Griffen, attending with his chaplain and a record congregation. Among these, of course, were many old friends, and, more especially, children and grandchildren of such. Quite a number of the Manions, and relatives, came to greet us after services, and the senior of them all -- the 93 year old Wm. Betsel. Mrs. Betsel was 87 and a blind invalid. She seemed quite appreciative of our visit and blessings. You re- member "Bill Betsel" who always drove the horses in threshing time. Besides visiting the Betsels, we went over and said the rosary at a certain Bowers home, whose oldest was laid out awaiting burial -drowned in Chicago a day or two before, on his seventh birthday. More about this late. Suffice it to say here that Mr. Bowers was not a Catholic, though I believe had taken instructions to some extent and seemed well disposed. The mother belonged some way to the O'Brien family and, consequently, seemed to hope that we might stay for the funeral and possibly conduct it, and offer the Mass. This we consented to do -- I ought to say, they arranged to do -- Maurice and Edward. I wished simply to leave everything to them and passively fall in line with what- ever they might wish to decide on -- begging the Good God to guide them, and us all, for the best. There was quite a crowd at the Rosary recital, and I believe, quite some edified. Returning from the Bowers, between 2 and 3 P.M., what seemed to the writer a happy feature of the day's program, was proposed. We were to go to "The Bluff". To him, that seemed to mean self-understoodly, "and to Trimbellle", and so it came. Fortunately, we took the old wagon road, rather than going a half mile north ot the Elsworth Highway, or down to that, following the course of the "Father of Waters". We were begin- ning to think we had made a mistake in not taking the latter for the 13 mile down-the-river trip, when, turning on a fairly trod road to the right, a neat little white house loomed through the trees (small bushes at my visit in 1878) and Fr. Maurice ex- claimed "Aunt Mary's old house!" "Sure enough" responded his neighbor. Fr. Edward got out and inquited how to reach the River Road down to Diamond Bluff. Fr. S. also went to the door, wish- ing to look in at least where nine and fifty years before he had spent happy days. Incidentally. it was during that visit of two weeks that he attended a court case in Prescott and took Judge Ross' chair while court was in session, hardly appreciating at that time why the court seemed amused. The late Judge Smith of Superior represented one side as opposed to a clever young lawyer named Wilson. However, we just waited until the senior judge returned before proceeding ... . . . Ha! Ha ! A modest little girl of about fifteen directed us to fol - low the main road until we came to a Highway "E", which would bring us right down to the River Road. Off we went, high speed, past Toohey's old place, and O'Brien's and Donovan's etc. Some of them (old places) still stand. Some have disappeared. Coming down the old sand hill to Big River Bottoms, we forgot our instruc- tions and followed the road down that old river bed. The river itself is a thing of past history. We only made about a half- mile when we found that instead of leading us to the River, our self-chosen road led us zig-zag up another hill -- scenery worth while -- and over a beautiful plateau-like section, till coming down to another cross-road, marked "E" we felt at ease again, knowing that now we'd reach the Bluff. Though no remark was made about it at the time, the beautiful valley down which said Highway "E" runs, is none other than what we used to know as "Manion's Ravine". I knew we had to come to that before we'd reach the Bluff. Well, we did reach the town at last, if it could any longer be called a town. We left the highway, crossed the railroad, did the whole place up and down, without finding any indication of where one might find a lunch. It was good that we were not very hungry, otherwise it would probably have been a story of "sour grapes". There was one, quite a BEER sign but we hardly appreciated such an invitation. In about ten minutes we were back on the highway, now bent on seeing the old farm and once familiar hills and valleys, etc. As a child I had never seen Diamond Bluff, but I had pic- tured it as quite a town at the mouth of the beautiful Trimbelle. I knew it had a store or two and that the Smith childrens' father had started another one, and that the steamboats used to stop there, but today's visit was to me rather a disappointment. We had gone perhaps eighty rods when we came to a road leading up to the left, which must have been the southern end of what we once upon a time called "the Main Road :. Here Good Providence would have us meet another Raphael. It was a handsome, rustic youth, driving some milch cows -- a happy sight in itself. We stopped beside him. "Where is the mouth of the Trimbelle" I asked. Pointing down the river to one of the many beautiful cliffs, he answered: "It's just behind yonder mountain-head, two miles further on your way." "God bless you, Boy" and on we sped. Then I remembered what had struck me as a sort of mystery passing down that way 25 years before. I had taken quite a risk, as some of my friends thought, when, coming back from the Golden Jubilee, in Seattle. I got off at St. Paul, deter - mined to say Holy Mass, even if the only train for Chicago that day, besides "our own" was due in 30 minutes, and I wanted to make Detroit next morning (Saturday). It had been raining ever since we left Seattle, (Tuesday evening), snowing, however, while crossing some of the Rocky Mountains: and now swirling clouds were actually twisting around the "Twin Cities" sky- scrapers. The Union Depot in St. Paul had been burned to the ground the day before yesterday, and, as yet, order and con- fusion were still wrangling for mastery. Your above referred to barefoot boy-friend -- now Sergeant Costello -- was on the scene, and gave me a warm greeting, mutually brief, however, for he was busy and I was in a hurry. He was prepared for the threatened storm and, as yet, I was able to dodge the drops or ignore them. HOLY MASS OFFERED -- TWO TRAINS HELD -- THANKS BE TO GOD Under such circumstances, I surely did hesitate: briefly, however, for there was really no time for deliberation. Having no umbrella, I started back to our train about to start off. then, again, seeing that it was not actually raining to speak of, I determined -- rain or shine -- train or no train, to go over to St. Mary's where Fr. Edward was assistant, and say Holy Mass and leave the rest to God. I had figured on catching the "Mil - waukee" scheduled to arrive from Seattle just an hour behind us, on the "N. P." but, we had lost thirty of those sixty minutes be- tween Minneapolis and the burned depot. The house-keeper at St. Mary's wondered that I was back so soon from the Solemnity. The Rt. Rev. Pastor was out on a sick- call, and I got to the Sacristy just in time for the last "Dominus Vobiscum", and final blessing of the 8 o'clock Mass. The young celebrant, too, was surprised at my early appearance; doubly so, on learning of my purpose to say Holy Mass and, even then, catch a train that day for Chicago. "If you were to start for the depot now, you might catch a train", he said, glancing at his watch, but, Thanks be to God, I said Holy Mass and made a short thanksgiving too. After breakfast, needless to say, no heavy one -- I lost no time in catching a trolley and getting over the half-mile or so to the station. "Is there any train for Chicago today?" I asked what seemed to be an official just waving a train backing in to stop. "Yes" he answered courteously "Here is one now". He hardly finished speaking, when, stopped was the train; on I stepped: and off went the "Burlington" at full speed; three hours late, its first stop at Point Douglas. I need not tell you what that meant to me. It took me past where I first saw the beauties of God's visible creation, down the Mississippi, where I played in the sand of its beautiful shore some four miles below; having crossed the mouth of the beautiful St. Croix and shot past Prescott where five of us had received Baptism. I certainly was not a tenth as grateful as I ought to have been, but I hope to be more so some day. I had reckoned, at all events, that it would please the Divine Lover of our poor souls and be good for mine especially to offer that Holy Mass; and that it would be a very easy thing for the Great God and Governor of the Universe to hold any train He might wish me to take. I hardly need to say that I asked HIM. Adored be His Holy Name! Now and forever. I do not remember that I was anxious about connections in Chicago, I probably was, more or less, seeing that we had to go so slowly in the rain, and for a time, through a fearful thun- derstorm. Just before reaching LaCrosse, we passed what seemed a victim of lightning, a burning farmhouse in the storm. Nearing the big city, five hours late, I asked the baggage- master about possible connections to Detroit. "The last train for Detroit is scheduled for some time about 6 P.M., and now it is nearly 10:30". Besides, that train was supposed to leave from a station about a twenty minute trolley ride from that of the "Burlington". Waiting for a transfer about half way over, it took me at least that, in the misty night air. How wonderful, however, and Thanks be to God; almost as though waiting for poor Father S., up went the megaphone the moment he entered: "All aboard! and Detroit. "All aboard" -- "Well, God bless them" he though -- "They'll wait now till I get my clergy-fare ticket." So they did. God bless them again. Now I could say Holy Mass at St. Bonaventure's in the morning, and what to me was imperative as Sacristan, I could reach Yonkers, N. Y. for the dedication of the new Sacred Heart Church next day. Thanks be to God, a million! Pardon this digression -- longer than it ought to be already -- but you'll be curious about the referred to mystery. Well, then as now, I was disappointed at no appearance of our beauti- ful Trimbelle, gracing Diamond Bluff, etc. However, notwith- standing the terrific storm that raged at the time of our passage that other trip, I had watched sharply and finally had the satis- faction of seeing what I concluded must be no other than the delightful little stream I looked for. Now I remembered my conclusion at that time; that it was about two miles below the Bluff. Pardon such digression. We had been making it a sort of rule to say the Rosary starting out on our longer trips. Today, however, we had gone a good twenty miles over hills and through beautiful valleys, and now speeding for said mountain-head, Fr. Maurice remarked: "Say, we've not said our Rosary. (Father) Barney it's your turn to lead . " "Okay" and the later started: "In the name You may wonder how we could pray under such circumstances. without distractions, etc. Well, I am not going to tell you the secret today, for the simple reason I do not know it my- self. Rather, we might ask: "Do such distractions really dis- please the Good God?" For myself, I do not think they do. Rather, I would answer, as I have occasion now and then to assure scrupulous souls: "No, Jesus is no crank. He knows that we are not angels, but poor sinners ; every one of us." At all events, as we rounded said mountain-head, such a distraction (which was probably common to four of us) came out in positive form. Father Edward, seeing the Trimbelle for the first time, and the exquisite landscape there for untold ages praising the Creator ahead of us, exclaimed simply and unqualifiedly: "This is beautiful!" Soon we were in what I recognized as Alihue, still neat and prim, but, like everything around, it seemed smaller than it was sixty years ago. You remember, of course, the frequent "revivals" in that little village when we were possibly their nearest Catholic neigh- bors, -- methodists, lutherans, etc., -- mostly honest, good Christians, as far as they knew. Perhaps a dozen children played on the green near a modest building apart as if waiting for some kind of sunday-school. They stopped and gazed our way, wondering, no doubt, at the two grey- beards in such never-before-seen garb. I was still leading the Rosary, or I think I would have greeted them with a blessing of some kind. As it was, I just wished it on them: "God bless you little Alihueians ! -- you and your dear elders; because in the face of the fearfully threatening avalanche of atheism, inundating the world these days, you are fostering at least something of the only practical remedy: RELIGION

God bless you and yours. Blessed be God for having created us and given us the true faith in His Redemption - and hope thereby in the final purpose of our existance, to know Him our Blessed Begin- ning, our Life and our All. Deo Gratias! ! ! I just read your interesting - awaited - letter for which many thanks. Poor, dear Jim: I sure would like to be with him; to cheer him and console and to "kid" him and wake him up - as I've had the privilege to do, thank God for quite a few in condition similar to his. Well after all maybe Jim is right in saying Fr. S. was there to see him. Possibly at least his Guarding Angel did the trick and gave him the consolation I surely would like to give. At all events I am there in spirit not a few times every day. Thank God for the faith and the mutual appreciation - fostered wherever real religion is found. Praised be the Lord for everything !.... It is a week now since your letter came and I started to answer at once. Its been on my mind continually. This at 3 O'C A.M. a call came and I asked, when they said, "an elderly person is dying", "is it a telegram ... ". I was at once wondering if it were from Seattle. ... I said: "Deo Gratias." It is now after vespers July 14th - Our dear St. Bonaventure's Day. I started a number of times yesterday and again this morning to finish the above and get it off and still it is not gore. I am still hoping it be God's will to spare our poor dear James. We are having "chapter here started early this A.M. - Election of a new Provincial and definitors, etc. It will probably be a week or more before its all over. We have close to fifty priests besides brothers attending .... . July 15. I had a "free Mass" Today which I offered quite specially for God's guidance of the Chapter and for dear Brother James. Am sending your letter on to Fr. Maurice. He seems doing well. Will probably go down to see him before long .... God's grace to all!
for speedy recovery, God willing - God bless you Emma, dear Sister Every time you think of opera- tion, Say "God help us" and then thank Him for it and for out-come
- with baby and all concerned - One holy Mass Specially God bless you Mildred.

I wrote Mrs. Baker and Mary of your difficulties but that you were keeping up. So do keep up as long as the dear Good God wills. But of course avoid anxiety - what glory that will be for each of us in eternity, just, in the end to have been able to say "Thou knowest O Jesus! Thy will be done."
Praised be Jesus and our Blessed Mother Mary who gave Him to us - and through Him became our own Blessed Mother Mary.

God bless you and yours. I hope you continue improving in body, mind and spirit, as last report from Mildred recently indicates you've been doing. Thanks be to God. How grateful we ought to be you and I that we are still "among the living"; still pilgrims able to merit for eternity, trying to follow thither at least in sight of the dearly de- serving, Divine Master. We, I say, because while it is something that at all event and everywhere as rational creatures men should do, you and I have special cause for thanking the Good God this year. I hardly need remind you of the marrow escapes you have had dur- ing the last ten months. Perhaps I ought rather refer to your threaten- ing experiences and conditions as someway pithed battles and, by the grace of God your victories; since you persevere in the Holy Faith. But I too had quite an experience in similar direction beginning last September about the 10th, with a severe case of "flue", together with a sort of vericose condition of ankle. While a number of my friends, both in the Hospital and outside seem to have considered my case "a close call to pneumonia, etc, I never felt that there was any immediate danger of colapse. Thanks be to God. To me it seemed about ten days of the really severest penance that the poor sinner Solanus had ever done and, therefore, since by God's grace he lived through it without complaint we have every reason to thank Heaven for the wonderful exper- ience. Deo Gratias. Now dear James :- since I received a hopeful letter from Fr. M. Joachim a few days ago, indicating a decided change in his attitude - a yearning to come back to the Monastery; and while you are still with us and able to appreciate, as I trust you will my little efforts, I am starting a conclusion to the description started before Fr. M.J. got sick; of Fr. Ed'wd's Jubilee and on that occasion our trip to "The Bluff" and old Trimbelle. Besides; while I find plenty of work to do here, nothing is so urgent that I cannot let it go till another day, for a sort of a double purpose; viz, to aford you a little entertain- ment and myself a form of recreation. - If I am not mistaken, I gave a copy of the above referred- to started-description to Mary and Helena when these two cousins were visiting me on their way to Montreal, Quebec, etc, a few years back. At all events when I get back to St. Bonaventure's I shall try and send you a copy of the same; for I am sure someone made a number of copies for me, seemingly anxious that even at that time I should finish it up as a worth-while whole. It will hardly be objectionable if we review a little of the description made before. So I'll start with our course of activity after the Solemn Mass of the Jubilee in Prescott (Wis.). Sunday August 22, the Octave of the Assumption, on which feast itself we had the first celebration in Superior, 165 miles to the N. Needless to say the neat little Church of St. Joseph looking down the rear on the Mississippi about 400 feet below, was filled to capa- city. Fr. Maurice J. and I had gone out to St. Mary's Big River the night before; Dean Conley having driven us down from St. Paul via River Falls, and Hudson. (Hardly necessary now to say who same D.C. was. It might've added somewhat to the already exquisit pleasure of the trip had we recognized in him what we only surmised at the time, a future nephew-in-law and ... Br. Jim's third son). We had offered our holy Masses out at said old St. Mary's where we older ones first went to holy Mass and to Catechism instructions, down to Maurice receiving First Holy Communion. We took the first scheduled Mass while the Rev. Pastor went to his mission several miles distant. I was inclined to envy him the privilege but felt that it was coming to him rather than to his younger brother but I quite enjoyed his nice little sermon. After our thanksgiving, etc, the pastor having returned reshot us down the Prescott-Elsworth Highway and before we knew it we were in the St. Joseph's sacristy vesting for solemn services, Rt. Rev. Bishop Griffin present. Fr. Solanus had been appointed several months before or about the same as appointed to give the sermon. It was his first time before a Bishop and I hardly remember if it was satisfactory. For himself it was far from what it ought to have been. Perhaps it was fortunate that he did not forsee what caused him quite a dissapointment before the Mass was over - No one except the Rev. Celebrant received Holy Communion: .... Otherwise everything went off without a hitch. Deo Gratias. But what a crowd waiting outside after the celebration in Church! One Mangan after an- other each with a family. Tim. and one or two of the others I recog- nized. And among the many others the senior of them all, now the 98 year-old Bill Betzel, if he still lives. He was 93 then, and his wife who was blind and an invalid 87 years-old wished to see us. So after dinner we visited her and she wept when we gave her cur blessing. From Betzel's we went over several blocks and prayed the rosary at the wake of a little Bower boy, a distant in-law drowned in Chicago a few days before. The child's mother, Kathleen, was a niece of John's first Wife Nellie (O"Brien); May their dear souls rest in peace! Fr. Maurice led the rosary. On our leaving there, it was de- cided that we take a "spin" down to Diamond Bluff. Of course I favored the proposition, because while "the Bluff" I am not sure if I sent you a copy of this letter some years ago or not. At all events I hope you like it. With my own it makes a double letter - worth while I hope.

I hope you are well. I've tried a number of times to start this card; now its 10:15 P.M. Was just talking with Mary. She is in great hopes that you will succeed in getting "Mother and Dad Jim" for a trip East. I think it would give (Jim at least) them another lease of ten yrs. Be sure and write them I said so. I've been wanting to write them so long. Have about sixty letters ahead to answer. Well! Well: so Annie O Brien is to celebrate her golden Wed'g. I remember her quite well - knew before she was married. I surely will remember them in Mass tomorrow

I hope you are well. I quite enjoyed your letter when I read it on Nov. 17 and again This A.M. when it came to my notice. Also did enjoy your dear Dad's discription of your trips to Burkhardt. Sorry he left out all about old Trimbelle. No doubt I ought to re- mind him as he proposed to continue ..... God bless you and yours. Mary is well; drops in or phones occasionally.

I just read your welcome card of the fourth and thank God you are well to write and get along so well. "Yes Msgr. Edw'd and Br. Owen joined us here the night of Jan. 25th. Grace "beat them to it" by plain from San Francisco and sur- prised them on their arrival in the Grand Central Depot - all coming together to the Monastery about 8 o'cl. Saturday 25th P.M. ) Grace phoned from E'd Sampson's and the telegram of her coming arrived Monday a.m. in the mail. The celebration - Solemn Mass, etc. was quite impressive as seemed to me. Only there not room for one half of the crowd that had come. I am sending you a few little cards that tell more in a few words that many letters might express. Thanks be to God for the privilege and for every detail and God bless our Guardian Angels - visible and invisible - each and all - for their part in the program . -

My Dear Sister Emma: - God bless you this joyful season of Eastertide and this even though in your condition the time must seem monotonous all the better chance to give a good sermon. The very best sermon one can give: - "How?" some one may ask, or on what subject! April 22 1949, Dear Emma: again; I am going to answer the above question by telling you of a dear class-mate of mine who was 84 last January 10th. About six months ago his sight became so poor that he had to give up saying holy Mass entirely. We all knew it: and oucourse we knew he would not like to hear such a decision. However, I was sort of deligated to break the unfavorable item. I asked him: " ... Well Father Damasus: How about that Sermon ?" "What sermon?" he enquired. We were all more or less anticipating indications of disapointment, etc. on his part; because not only was his sight failing seriously but his rearing likewise. I said: "Well Fr. D. its the last sermon any of us will be able to give and its on patience and holy resignation." Thanks be to God; he received the announcement without the least change of countenance and has been an esample of patience and resignation ever since - a real sermon and edification to the 30 novices and to us all. Never a complaint! I hope Dear Sister that you will forgive me for not writing you. I hav stated a number of times to do so; but honestly more friquently there are so many things it seems I ought to do and do not get time that I feel I get no where and do seemingly nothing. .... I am sure Fr. Edw'd has written of Fr.E.J.'s peaceful and beautiful death and really joyful, solem Mass and funeral. Every one seemed happy. As we followed His Excellency the Bishop from the cemetery one of the fifteen priest half-exclaimd-"This is more like a bridal affair than a funeral." ... Keep courage; rather confidence in God, which is courage divinely reenforced.

Mrs. James Casey - for speedy health improvement, God willing - emergency - special - member. February 18th 1948 God bless you Sister, Emma Casey "Courage is half the battle" Keep it up. Confidence in God is courage infinitely reinforced by God's grace to be always fostered - the very soul of prayer.
